meta.title: Numu Yadooape (Northern Paiute Language)
meta.notes: Disc 4 is the most grammar-focused disc in the series. It introduces two full verb paradigms (jump, see/look), applied color usage for red, body condition phrases (Numma), yes/no question formation with ha'a, and a systematic survey of five grammatical suffixes (-kwu, -hookwu, -pu, -ku, -kooha). The disc closes with two sentence structure lessons using word-by-word component glosses. Many base verbs introduced here (Hebe, Mea, Saa, Tumu, Tubo, Yaga, etc.) appear across multiple suffix lessons, making this disc a core grammar reference layer for the app.

elongated_sounds.description: Doubled letters indicate sounds held longer: aa, ee, mm, nn

glottal_stop.description: Apostrophe marks a split-second interruption of breath and sound. Voiceless glottal.

consonants.sound_description: s sound, only used in few words
either like English 's' (as in silly) or like English 'sh' (as in shop). If next to 'e' or 'i', sounds like 'sh'
like 'w' in 'Will' but softer, between 'm' and 'w'

grammar_suffix_note: Disc 4 systematically documents five grammatical suffixes that modify verb meaning. -kwu (future tense): attaches to verb root to indicate future action. -hookwu (present/immediate tense): attaches with glottal stop to indicate imminent or ongoing action; source labels this 'present tense' but conjugations translate as 'will/going to', suggesting it marks near-future or intended action. -pu (past tense): attaches to verb root to indicate completed action. -ku (causative/benefactive): marks that the action is done for or to someone else; causes verb action to occur on behalf of another. -kooha (inchoative): marks the beginning or restart of an action — 'start to [verb]'. Many of the same base verbs appear across all five suffix lessons, making these lessons well-suited for a paradigm-table view in the app.

lessons.title: All about Jump
lessons.notes: Full paradigm for Nadakwunae (jump). Parallel in structure to Disc 3 Lesson 28 (All About Eating / Tuka). Encodes aspect, directionality, number (two / group), and modality (try, hasn't yet, might). The four phrase_forms at the bottom use auxiliary words (Too'e, Kisoo, Sumuna) to modify the verb. Note: Kisoo Nadakwuna'e uses a slight spelling variant of the root (Nadakwuna'e vs Nadakwunae) — verify against audio.

lessons.title: The Color Red
lessons.notes: Applied usage lesson for the color red (root: Atsa-, adjective form: Atsakweta). Builds directly on the color morphology system documented in Disc 3 Lesson 22. Entries are numbered phrases and sentences demonstrating red in varied grammatical roles — as subject, object, modifier, compound, and predicate. Entry 6 flag: source prints 'Atsakwedu' (missing 't') — likely a print error for 'Atsakwetadu'; verify against audio. Entry 23 (Atsabana = flicker) refers to the northern flicker bird, which has red coloring — cross-reference with Disc 3 blends section where Atsabana also appears as a blend example.

lessons.title: Poone [see, watch, look]
lessons.notes: Full paradigm for Poone (see/look/watch). Parallel structure to Disc 3 Lesson 28 (Tuka/eat) and Disc 4 Lesson 33 (Nadakwunae/jump). Encodes posture during action (sitting, standing, laying), continuity, number (two, group), directionality (come to see, went and returned), and modality (might see, want to see, ask to see). Entry 21 includes a full example sentence. Flag: entries 1 and 5 are both printed as 'Poonekwu' — entry 1 is labeled 'will or going to see [future tense]' and entry 5 as 'going to see' with no tense label. May be a print duplicate or a subtle distinction; verify against audio.

lessons.title: Numma [body condition]
lessons.notes: Numma is a broad-meaning word covering hurt, sick, ache, or any kind of feeling or bodily condition. Lesson is presented as 18 contextual phrases and sentences. Flag on entry 13: source begins the sentence with 'How' — this may be a Numu discourse particle or an artifact of the print layout; verify against audio. Nummadu (entry 14) = the sick person (noun form). Nummakwu (entry 11) = will feel better (future tense suffix -kwu applied). Numma'hoo (entries 9-10) = got sick (just-past form). Numma'hoodooa (entry 15) = might get sick.

lessons.title: ha'a [questions]
lessons.notes: Ha'a is described as a special form to ask questions — functions as a yes/no question marker inserted into a statement to form a question. It appears immediately after the subject (U ha'a = do you...?) or after a demonstrative (Esoo ha'a = is this...?). 23 example questions across diverse contexts. Entry 19 has a trailing slash in the source (Haga ha'a U Poonegena? /) — print artifact; transcribed as question mark. Vocabulary appearing here that cross-references other lessons: Tukapu (ate — Disc 3 Tuka paradigm), Poonegena (come to see — Disc 4 Lesson 35), Tumukwu (going to buy — Disc 4 Lesson 38).

are you guys ready / you all ready?

lessons.title: -kwu [future tense]
lessons.suffix_meaning: future tense — indicates action that will happen
lessons.notes: 21 verb roots shown with -kwu suffix applied. The suffix attaches directly to the end of the verb root. Entry 21 (Hoobea = song) is notable: the combined form is Hoobeadookwu rather than *Hoobeakwu — a compound construction using an intermediate -doo- element likely meaning 'make' (will make song). Flag for app grammar layer: this may indicate Hoobea is a noun (song), not a verb root, and requires a mediating verb to take tense suffixes.

suffix_entries.notes: Intermediate -doo- element in combined form (not plain -kwu attachment) — likely a compound 'make-song-future'; Hoobea may be a noun requiring a mediating verb to take tense suffixes. Flag for grammar layer.

lessons.title: -hookwu [present tense]
lessons.suffix_meaning: present / near-future tense — indicates imminent or intended action
lessons.notes: 21 verb roots shown with -hookwu suffix applied via glottal stop + hookwu (e.g., Tuka + 'hookwu = Tuka'hookwu). Source labels this 'present tense' but all translations read as 'will / going to', suggesting -hookwu marks near-future or intended action rather than ongoing present. Contrast with -kwu (Lesson 38) which is labeled 'future tense' — the distinction appears to be immediacy of the intended action. Two flags: (1) Entry 11: base form Tubo (write) — combined form printed as Tobo'hookwu, showing a vowel change u→o; verify against audio and cross-reference with Lesson 40 -pu entries where 'to write' appears as Tupo. (2) Entry 19: Masua (plant) — combined form printed as Masua'hokwu, missing one 'o' vs the -hookwu pattern; likely print error.

suffix_entries.notes: Vowel change in root: Tubo → Tobo in combined form. Verify against audio. Also see Lesson 40 entry 4 where 'to write' appears as Tupo.
Source prints Masua'hokwu — likely print error for Masua'hookwu (one 'o' missing); verify against audio

lessons.title: -pu [past tense]
lessons.notes: 20 verb roots with -pu suffix. The suffix attaches directly to the verb root. Two flags requiring audio verification: (1) Entry 4 lists base form as 'Tupo' for 'to write', but Lesson 38 (-kwu) and Lesson 42 (-kooha) both use 'Tubo' for write — Tupo may be a print error for Tubo, or a distinct related form; verify against audio. (2) Entry 11: source prints 'bloaded' — clearly a typo for 'bloated'; corrected in transcription. Entry 15 (Tohatae = state of being white) is interesting — past tense form 'faded' suggests Tohatae encodes a whiteness/fading state rather than the base color white (Tohakweta from Disc 3).

suffix_entries.notes: Source prints Tupo for 'write'; Lessons 38 and 42 use Tubo for the same meaning. Possible print error. Verify against audio.

lessons.title: -ku ending
lessons.suffix_meaning: causative / benefactive — when somebody does the verb action for somebody else, causing verb action to occur
lessons.notes: 18 verb roots with -ku suffix. Most attach cleanly (Saa + -ku = Saaku, Tumu + -ku = Tumuku). However, two entries show significant base-form transformation: (1) Entry 2: Wunu [stand] + -ku = Tsakwunuku — the prefix Tsa- is added; (2) Entry 6: Mea [go] + -ku = Tsameaku — again Tsa- prefix appears with vowel modification. This Tsa- element may be a productive applicative or causative morpheme that appears when -ku is applied to certain motion/posture verbs. Flag both for grammar layer documentation and audio verification.

suffix_entries.notes: Base transforms significantly: Wunu + -ku yields Tsakwunuku with Tsa- prefix and -kw- infix. Verify against audio; may indicate a causative morpheme Tsa-.
Base transforms: Mea + -ku yields Tsameaku with Tsa- prefix. Same Tsa- morpheme as entry 2. Verify against audio.

lessons.title: -kooha ending
lessons.suffix_meaning: inchoative — restart or beginning of action; 'start to [verb]'
lessons.notes: 21 verb roots with -kooha suffix. Most attach via glottal stop + kooha (e.g., Yaga'kooha). Cross-reference: Nadakwunaekooha (started jumping) appeared in Lesson 33 verb paradigm — confirms -kooha pattern. Flag: Entry 19 (Tohatae = fade) — combined form printed as Tohataekooha without apostrophe separator, while all other entries use apostrophe (e.g., Yaga'kooha). May be a print inconsistency; verify against audio. Note the -kooha lesson label is 'restart action' suggesting this suffix applies when resuming a previously stopped action, not just any beginning.

suffix_entries.notes: Source prints Tohataekooha without apostrophe separator, unlike all other entries in this lesson which use glottal stop + kooha. Possible print inconsistency; verify against audio.

lessons.title: Sentence I
lessons.notes: 14 example sentences with word-by-word component glosses. Source presents each sentence with English word labels above, the Numu sentence in bold below, and the full English translation on the right. Demonstrates location markers (Sawabedooha = sagebrush-under, Kibagooba = mountain-on top, Sungabekwae = tree-in), progressive aspect (-wunu ending on Tuka and Maka), possessive family terms (Moo'a = mother's mother/grandma, Pedoo'o = mother's sister/aunt), and subject/object word order. Soo identifies the subject of a sentence; Ka identifies the object.

lessons.title: Sentence II
lessons.notes: 11 example sentences continuing from Lesson 43. Source reinforces that Soo identifies the subject and Ka identifies the object of a sentence. Introduces Yukwe (two sitting), Wanga'a (younger brother), Pedoo'o (mother's sister/aunt). The final sentence is a math/riddle sentence: three crows on a fence, one flies off — how many are left? Introduces several new vocabulary items: Tooebetse'e (young man), Moogoosoo (lizard), Muhagoobakwae (moon-over), Koodeagooba (fence-on top), Yotse'hooka (fly). Note: two different forms for 'two' appear across entries 6 and 9 — Wahoo vs Wa'hoo; compare also Waha'yoo (entry 8) — may reflect different grammatical forms or counting contexts; verify across Disc 2 Numbers lesson.
